items.title: Paul Basu curates On Paradise at Oxford's new White Box gallery
items.summary: The Oxford anthropologist and Pitt Rivers curator has curated the inaugural exhibition at the Schwarzman Centre's White Box, exploring lost edens and hoped-for utopias (2 October to 6 December).

items.title: Amazonian animism meets the "Rights of Nature" at the RAI Myers Lecture
items.summary: Aparecida Vilaça of the Museu Nacional, Rio de Janeiro, gave this year's Myers Lecture at King's College London following the RAI AGM, where the 2026 RAI medals and awards were also announced.

items.title: Six senior promotions at UCL Anthropology
items.summary: Promotions recognise colleagues working across social, biological, environmental and evolutionary anthropology, from fiscal relations and the state to conservation and the evolution of human birth.

items.title: Cambridge celebrates postgraduate fieldwork photography
items.summary: PhD students Alejandro Porcel Arraut and Zihan Xu share first place in the department's Postgraduate Photography Celebration.

items.title: London Anthropology Day welcomes the next generation
items.summary: The annual taster day gives school students considering university a first experience of anthropology lectures, workshops and conversations with current students.

items.title: UCL alumna Myriam Lamrani shares the 2026 Edie Turner First Book Prize
items.summary: Lamrani's first book, The Intimacy of Images, has been co-awarded this year's Edie Turner First Book Prize.

items.title: When AI breaks your heart
items.summary: Manchester digital anthropologist Jennifer Cearns studies people's romantic bonds with AI 'soulmates' and the grief that follows when a chatbot changes or shuts down.

items.title: Durham anthropologists join a £7m project to rethink energy storage
items.summary: Anthropology works with engineering and chemistry in EleComp, an EPSRC programme grant with Imperial and Bristol on materials that store energy.

items.title: Why milk is never just milk
items.summary: Oxford anthropology alum JC Niala features in a new BBC Ideas film on the history, politics and industry behind an everyday drink.

items.title: Wellcome award for research on disability and China's one-child policy
items.summary: Jingxian Wang at King's Lau China Institute will draw on medical anthropology and disability studies to examine a hidden legacy of the policy.

items.title: Why some chimpanzee mothers carry their dead infants for months
items.summary: Oxford research in Biology Letters links carrying to the mother-infant bond, with cause of death the most consistent predictor of how long it lasts.

items.title: Can South Asia's student uprisings build solidarity across borders?
items.summary: Durham political anthropologist Nayanika Mookherjee argues in The Wire and Bangladesh's New Age that youth protests share struggles over jobs, education, free expression and state power, and could link up despite regional tensions.

items.title: Georgina Born convenes an international summit on public service media
items.summary: The UCL anthropologist has organised an international summit on the future of public service media.

items.title: St Andrews opens virtual fellowships for scholars in Gaza
items.summary: The Department of Social Anthropology is offering three one-term Virtual Fellowships in 2026/27 for Palestinian scholars based in Gaza.

items.title: ERC funds Toby Kelly's study of private detectives
items.summary: Edinburgh anthropologist Professor Toby Kelly has won European Research Council funding for a study of private detectives.

items.title: Monkey friendships with other animals and the origins of pet-keeping
items.summary: An international study mapping primates' friendships with dogs, deer and pigs suggests human-animal companionship may have deep evolutionary roots.

items.title: Rebecca Cassidy and Joel Robbins elected Fellows of the British Academy
items.summary: The two Cambridge anthropologists are among 92 scholars elected to the Fellowship for 2026.

items.title: Teaching knife-wound analysis without animal bones
items.summary: Forensic research at Liverpool John Moores tests whether non-animal materials can stand in for bone when studying cut marks.

items.title: Matei Candea publishes an anthropology of free speech
items.summary: Reason, Carnival and Honour (Penguin), by Cambridge's Head of Department, compares how free speech is understood and argued over around the world.

items.title: Ruby Livingston wins the 2026 Sue Benson Prize
items.summary: Cambridge's annual prize for the most outstanding undergraduate dissertation in social anthropology goes to Ruby Livingston of Christ's College.

items.title: The health impacts of incarceration in Latin America
items.summary: UCL's Caroline Parker and Daniela Larrain publish new research on how imprisonment affects health in Latin America.

items.title: Emma Tarlo elected Fellow of the British Academy
items.summary: Goldsmiths' Emeritus Professor of Anthropology is among this year's 92 new Fellows.

items.title: Marcus Banks's writings on Jainism collected in a posthumous volume
items.summary: Jainism as Social and Visual Practice gathers the late Oxford visual anthropologist's ethnographic work, edited by John E. Cort, David Zeitlyn and Chihab El Khachab.

items.title: Why do free speech debates make us so angry?
items.summary: In the Guardian, Cambridge anthropologist Matei Candea argues that behind fights over definitions and rules, people are often really arguing about character.

items.title: What is 'Chrislam'?
items.summary: SOAS anthropologist Marloes Janson writes in The Conversation (France) on how people in Lagos combine religious traditions in search of health and prosperity.

items.title: ERC Advanced Grant for Christos Lynteris: Zoonosis Before Bacteriology
items.summary: The St Andrews anthropologist has won a European Research Council Advanced Grant for a project on understandings of zoonotic disease before bacteriology. In September he also received a BA/Leverhulme grant comparing French and British colonial maps of endemic disease.

items.title: Understanding and stewarding the Arctic
items.summary: Durham's Simone Abram joined geographers and lawyers in a public Chancellor-in-Conversation event on climate change and the four million people who live in the Arctic.

items.title: Why more births now end in caesarean section
items.summary: Drawing on fieldwork in Bangladesh, Durham researcher Halima Akhter shows how fear, trust in doctors and worries about blame push caesarean rates up, and how much of the long recovery falls on families.

items.title: Freedom of speech takes many forms, and they are always cultural
items.summary: Matei Candea writes in The Conversation that there have always been competing ideas of what it means to speak freely.

items.title: Baby slings: what the evidence says
items.summary: Durham PhD researcher Sophie Lovell-Kennedy reviews the evidence on benefits, risks and safe use, and the gaps in guidance for parents.

items.title: A ten-point manifesto for anthropology's future
items.summary: Anthropologists from industry, policy and academia met at UCL East to debate AI, the public good and how universities prepare anthropologists for work beyond academia. Contributors included Gillian Tett.

items.title: Taking conservation field staff seriously as experts
items.summary: Liana Chua argues in Field Reflections, a collection of accounts from 17 NGO staff in Indonesian Borneo, that frontline workers are experts in community engagement.

items.title: Nomi Dave named Evans-Pritchard Lecturer for 2026-27
items.summary: Oxford has appointed the anthropologist of sound, voice, violence and law, author of The Revolution's Echoes on music and politics in Guinea.

items.title: St Andrews hosts a workshop on just plastic waste management
items.summary: The international workshop (13 to 14 June) brought academics, policymakers, industry and waste picker representatives together on fairer, more sustainable plastic waste systems.

items.title: Why births have fallen to a fifty-year low
items.summary: Oxford anthropologist Dr Paula Shepard commented for the BBC on what lies behind the UK's falling birth rate and how people weigh the decision to have children.

items.title: Disease stigma in Colombia's coca and coffee borderlands
items.summary: In American Ethnologist, Javier Lezaun and Lina Pinto-García show how cutaneous leishmaniasis takes on very different meanings in coca- and coffee-growing areas.

items.title: Hidden cognitive strengths in children growing up in adversity
items.summary: Doctoral research by Gabriele Paone pairs standard memory tests with tasks adapted to social memory, revealing skills conventional tests can miss.

items.title: The case for maintenance in a culture obsessed with change
items.summary: Durham anthropologists Tom Yarrow and Paolo Heywood use the work of stonemasons to argue that keeping things going is skilled, demanding labour that politics too often mistakes for doing nothing.

items.title: Solving the puzzle of human right-handedness
items.summary: Research by Thomas Püschel and Rachel Hurwitz (Oxford) with Chris Venditti (Reading) offers an evolutionary account of why most people favour their right hand.

items.title: Why male primates may have grown bigger than females
items.summary: Oxford research rethinks sexual selection, suggesting competition between neighbouring groups helped drive size differences between the sexes.

items.title: Disobedient Buildings: life in London's ageing tower blocks
items.summary: Inge Daniels launches a digital exhibition, five years in the making, on the love and worry of tower block living, told through residents' own postcards.

items.title: Were early human societies equal?
items.summary: Bristol's Kit Opie and Scott Claessens introduce The Origins of Inequality, a project asking when and why inequality took hold across cultures.

items.title: Chimpanzees in Rwanda seem to plan ahead for bad weather
items.summary: A project led by Cyril Grueter finds chimpanzees in Nyungwe National Park adjust how they build nests in anticipation of the weather.

items.title: New book: Constructing the Achievement State
items.summary: Chihab El Khachab shows how low- and mid-ranking bureaucrats represented and embodied the Egyptian state under Nasser.

items.title: Marcio Goldman gives the 2026 Peter Gow Memorial Lecture
items.summary: The Museu Nacional anthropologist lectured at St Andrews on ethnographic theory and its history under the title "Nothing is simple".

items.title: New book: How Plague Got Rats
items.summary: Christos Lynteris traces how the rat, only recently, became the symbol of plague, drawing on six years of Wellcome-funded research.

items.title: New book: From the Heart of Kulob
items.summary: Diana Ibañez-Tirado's ethnography of southern Tajikistan explores how ordinary Kulobis build dignified, moral and joyful lives despite hardship.

items.title: The imperilled presence of Afghans in Pakistan
items.summary: In Current History, Sussex's Magnus Marsden examines how hardening borders and deportations are straining long-standing ties across Central and South Asia.

items.title: Why do some people eat soil?
items.summary: Durham PhD researcher Zander Simpson traces geophagy from deep prehistory to prison diets and modern tasting menus, weighing up its cultural meanings and health risks.

items.title: Oxford tops the 2026 QS ranking for anthropology
items.summary: The School of Anthropology and Museum Ethnography is ranked first in the world for the subject in this year's QS World University Rankings.

items.title: How to spot the use and abuse of the word 'context'
items.summary: Durham anthropologist Paolo Heywood asks what it really means to understand something "in context", and how the appeal gets used in arguments.

items.title: The Plastic Divide: how carrier bag bans hit the poorest
items.summary: After nine months in Dar es Salaam, Manchester anthropologist Declan Murray shows how East Africa's plastic bag bans can make life harder for the people they aim to protect.

items.title: Remembering Tim Allen (1956-2026)
items.summary: LSE mourns its Professor in Development Anthropology and founding director of the Firoz Lalji Institute for Africa, known for his ethnographic work across East Africa.

items.title: Young people turning to AI chatbots as surrogate friends
items.summary: Manchester anthropologist Jennifer Cearns gave the BBC her analysis of why young people in the North West are coming to rely on AI companions, and the risks involved.

items.title: Xolu Dakar bi: an exhibition on life in a Dakar settlement facing resettlement
items.summary: Anna Wood curated the exhibition with Dakar photographers Djibril Dramé and Katia Golovko, exploring everyday life and uncertainty as the city transforms.

items.title: Black women's knowledge of racial inequality in maternity care
items.summary: Cambridge anthropologist Caroline Bazambanza examines how Black women make sense of inequality in maternity care, and why their knowledge is so often ignored.

items.title: Alpa Shah on the legacy of Jaipal Singh Munda
items.summary: Oxford's Professor of Social Anthropology writes in Outlook India on the Adivasi leader, Olympian and Constituent Assembly member, and what his politics mean today.

items.title: Returning to Daraa, after exile and revolution
items.summary: Sussex anthropologist Charlotte Al-Khalili's photo essay in American Anthropologist reflects on homecoming, memory and rebuilding among ruins in Syria.

items.title: Medieval kings and bishops reinterred at Winchester Cathedral
items.summary: After more than a decade of osteological and DNA work involving University of Winchester specialists, jumbled royal remains have been reassembled and reinterred.

items.title: New podcast: Fieldnotes from Sussex Anthropology
items.summary: Hosted by Dr Syeda Sana Batool, the series ranges across trade, fieldwork, memory, therapy and AI in accessible conversations with Sussex anthropologists.

items.title: Dream State: how the Shuar reinvented the state from within
items.summary: In the Cambridge Alumni Magazine, Natalia Buitron describes how an Amazonian people forced into cooperatives and state structures reworked them on their own terms.

items.title: Peasants to Paupers: the human toll of Kenya's property boom
items.summary: Peter Lockwood's new book tells the stories of people on Nairobi's expanding edges, where land, class and kinship are being transformed.
